transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to restore White House access to three media
organizations.
CNN, MS Now and Politico had sued, saying President Trump's abrupt decision to ban them
was because he didn't like them or their content, and that was a First Amendment violation.
NPR's David Falkenflick reports the judge cited an additional reason for his decision.
Judge Kelly ruled that there was a clear violation of these institutions due process rights.
That's part of the Fifth Amendment.
That is, you can't have something taken away from you without being told ahead of time
and being given a chance to weigh in and even appeal that decision.
He said the government clearly deprived them of that.
And he dismissed the argument that the three outlets had jeopardized national security,
which the administration's lawyers from the Justice Department had argued.
NPR's David Falkenflick reporting.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told the United Nations Russia's war will soon
spread to other parts of Europe.
NPR's Joanna Kekisis reports he called on allies to force the Kremlin to end the war
before another brutal winter starts.
Zelensky said that more than 248,000 Russian soldiers had been killed or wounded in Ukraine
over the last eight months.
We have an archive of drone videos, videos showing thousands and thousands of Russians
losing their lives in kill zones.
Zelensky also detailed how Russia's war is hurting the world.
He talked about grain shortages, rising fuel prices, and the race to develop even more lethal
drone warfare.
As early as next year, there is already a real possibility that AI, not only people,
will begin to decide what happens on the battlefield.
We need peace, he said, before we reach that point.
Joanna Kekisis, NPR News, Cave.
The FBI's jobs portal remains down.
The bureau is investigating claims that hackers breached the bureau's computer systems and
stole data on FBI employees.
NPR's Ryan Lucas reports this comes a day after the hacking group SHINee Hunter's claimed
responsibility.
The FBI says in a statement posted on X that it is aware of the cybercriminal group's claims
to have compromised the FBI jobs portal and stolen personal information of FBI employees.
The bureau says the point of the hack is still undetermined, but it says the FBI is aggressively
investigating and actively working to shore up any potential risk.
The stolen information allegedly includes names of current and former FBI employees,
as well as their home addresses and phone numbers.
The breach raises significant counterintelligence concerns for the nation's premier law enforcement
agency.
Ryan Lucas, NPR News, Washington.
This is NPR.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says he spoke to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.
That's after it was revealed the tech company's AI agent breached an Australian government
health care site last June.
The Australian leader is angry because OpenAI did not inform his government in a timely
manner.
He says his government is opening an investigation.
AI assistants are becoming increasingly popular as the technology grows more sophisticated.
NPR's Windsor Johnston reports their expanding reach is raising questions about privacy, accountability
and how much control people should hand over to a bot.
The more an AI assistant can do, the more access it may need to things like email, calendars,
travel accounts and banking information.
Cornell University tech policy professor Sarah Krepp says problems can arise when those systems
are given too much freedom to act.
They're very literal, but they don't understand kind of the broader human intent behind it.
And so that's where you get these disconnects between the limits of what the agent would
do and what it actually does.
A mistake could mean changing a reservation, sending an ill-considered email or taking
another action before the user ever sees it.
Windsor Johnston, NPR News.
Researchers have issued a hurricane watch for the Big Island of Hawaii.
Tropical storm NOLO is expected to become a hurricane, but it's not expected to make
landfall.
It is still likely to drop more than two feet of rain on some parts of Hawaii.
This is NPR.
